1Report 05: the block model

1.1The sentence about APL, rewritten

Old: "APL is one cell whose activity, for each odor, is the average response of the KCs. It inhibits every KC by subtracting a fixed multiple of that activity."

New: "APL is modelled as a single unit with one activity level per odor. Every KC excites APL, so this activity is the mean response of all KCs to that odor. APL then inhibits every KC equally: it subtracts its activity times a gain aaa from each KC's input. The gain is the same for every odor, but the inhibition is not, because APL's activity is higher for odors that drive more KCs."

1.2Why the bouton and claw weights of P and L are counted per synapse

In versions P and L, inhibition does not subtract from the KC. It divides the input that glomerulus ggg sends to every KC by 1+b p~g Ao1 + b\,\tilde p_g\,A_o1+bp~​g​Ao​. So p~g\tilde p_gp~​g​ has to answer one question: how strongly is each unit of ggg's input inhibited? Raw APL synapse counts answer a different question, because big glomeruli have more of everything. DC1 has 6,125 PN→KC synapses and VA1v 1,965. If both had the same number of APL→PN synapses per bouton, DC1 would still have about 3 times as many in total. The size of a glomerulus's input already enters the model through WkgW_{kg}Wkg​. Using raw APL counts would count size a second time and make big glomeruli look strongly inhibited simply because they are big. Dividing by the excitatory synapses removes that: pgp_gpg​ is the number of APL synapses that each PN→KC synapse of ggg "sees".

(In the sentence you copied, the symbol ggg is typeset as math, which is why it dropped out of the copied text as "glomerulus 's".)

1.3Why the input weights are divided by all of the KC's claw PN synapses

Dividing by the KC's total makes its drive xkox_{ko}xko​ a weighted average of its glomeruli's responses, so every KC's drive is on the same scale whatever its size. Without it, the drive would be ∑gnkg rgo\sum_g n_{kg}\,r_{go}∑g​nkg​rgo​, which grows with the number of synapses. KCs differ a lot in that number: hemibrain KCs have a median of 89 claw PN synapses (5–95% 32–192), and γ KCs have about twice as many as the others (151 on average, against 75 for αβ and 70 for α′β′). With raw counts and one threshold, γ KCs would take most of the responses. The averaging assumes that a KC with more input synapses also needs more input to reach threshold, which is roughly what a larger dendrite (lower input resistance) does.

The denominator also includes claws whose main PN is not in the response table or is multiglomerular. Those claws count as input of 0, so a KC whose claws come mostly from unmeasured glomeruli gets a smaller drive, instead of having its few measured claws scaled up.

This is a modelling choice, and the data do not settle it. The rebuilt Report 05 will add two alternatives so the effect can be seen: raw synapse counts (Wkg=nkgW_{kg} = n_{kg}Wkg​=nkg​, one threshold), and equal weight per claw (WkgW_{kg}Wkg​ = share of the KC's claws from ggg).

1.4What each number in "Results of the prediction run" is

"r" in Report 05 is always the Pearson correlation. Spearman (rank) correlations are written ρ\rhoρ or ρs\rho_sρs​ in all reports (for example the rank order in Reports 06 and 09). The rebuilt reports will spell out "Pearson r" or "Spearman ρ" each time.

The r = 0.99 is not a correlation between KC responses and ORN responses. "With ORN input" only says which response table drove the model (as opposed to GH146). The correlation is over odors, between how many KCs an odor drives with APL blocked and how many more KCs respond when APL is blocked.

1.5Does similarity rise most for pairs of strong odors? (ms included)

The claim holds: pairs of strongly driven odors gain the most similarity (Spearman ρ = 0.71 with ORN input, 0.65 with GH146). The pairs with ms sit at ΔS ≈ 0 with ORN input, because ms barely drives any KC: its ORN responses are weak, and with one shared threshold almost no KC reaches it. This is a property of the Report 05 setup only. From Report 07 on, each odor is pinned to its TNT fraction (ms: 11.6% of units), so ms is fully part of every comparison there.

In the rebuilt Report 05, ms stays in every figure and table. Where its similarity is undefined (no KC responds), the cell is marked as such instead of being dropped.

1.6What goes into the rebuilt Report 05

  • PN-level transformation (item 1): ORN → PN through the divisive normalization of Olsen et al. (2010), as used in Kennedy's model (2019, "Learning with naturalistic odor representations in a dynamic model of the Drosophila olfactory system"). Its output is compared with the GH146 results. If you meant a different Kennedy paper, tell me.
  • Negative rgor_{go}rgo​ (item 4): a version that keeps inhibitory glomerular responses instead of setting them to 0.
  • Inhibition on both PNs and KCs (item 5): APL subtracts from KCs and divides bouton input per glomerulus at the same time, with the per-glomerulus bouton weights (like M, with C-style per-KC weights on the KC side).
  • Figures 8 and 9 for every version (item 8), each caption stating the mean change in similarity with and without inhibition, and a comparison of every version with U.
  • Marked pairs (item 9): in the ΔS\Delta SΔS heat maps, the pairs that change most and least are outlined.
  • Data at the end (item 10): the response-similarity heat maps of the recordings (Report 06, Figure 3), for direct comparison.
  • The two alternative WWW normalizations above, and the sentence rewrite.

2Report 06: the recordings

Units. The responses are FC z-scores (fc_zscore). The rebuilt report says so, and "responding" means a response above 1 z-score unit.

2.1What the per-odor effect is, and what it means mechanistically

The fit ΔSab≈μ+ea+eb\Delta S_{ab} \approx \mu + e_a + e_bΔSab​≈μ+ea​+eb​ says: the change of a pair is the average change, plus a bit that belongs to each of its two odors. eae_aea​ is how much more (or less) the pairs that contain odor aaa change than the average pair. For example eebe_{\text{eb}}eeb​ = +0.050: pairs with eb gain about 0.05 more cosine similarity than average when APL is blocked, whatever the partner. An odor with a large eae_aea​ has its whole row of the similarity matrix move up.

Mechanism: chance overlap. When an odor drives more units, it shares more responding units with every other odor just by chance (Report 08, Step 2: two unrelated 0/1 codes have cosine papb\sqrt{p_a p_b}pa​pb​​). So an odor that gains many responders when APL is blocked should gain similarity with all partners, which is exactly a large eae_aea​. This can be tested on the data alone: compute the chance overlap papb\sqrt{p_a p_b}pa​pb​​ from each recording's fractions responding, take its change TNT − TNT3c, fit the same additive model to it, and compare its per-odor effects with the real eae_aea​.

The per-odor effects follow chance overlap (Spearman ρ = 0.73). They also follow how many units an odor drives in TNT (ρ = 0.76) and how many it gains (TNT − TNT3c, ρ = 0.73), but not the ratio TNT ÷ TNT3c (ρ = 0.23). So the per-odor part of the change is mostly the arithmetic of denser codes: odors that drive many units in TNT, such as eb, 2h and IaA, overlap more with everything. -aPine and euc gain the fewest responding units when APL is blocked (2.5 and 4.0 percentage points, against 5.7–13.9 for the other odors) and have the most negative effects.

3Report 07: pinning and the comparison

3.1Equation 1 with numbers: the per-odor input gain

The goal of pinning is that, with APL blocked, the model drives exactly the fraction of KCs that TNT drives for each odor. The threshold is fixed at θ = 1, and each odor's input is multiplied by a gain gog_ogo​ chosen so that the right number of KCs end up above 1. Here is the calculation for a mock mushroom body of 10 KCs and one odor that drives 20% of units in TNT:

  • 1. Unscaled drives ∑gWkgrgo\sum_g W_{kg} r_{go}∑g​Wkg​rgo​ of the 10 KCs: 0.12, 0.30, 0.05, 0.42, 0.22, 0.18, 0.60, 0.35, 0.08, 0.50.
  • 2. Sort them: 0.05, 0.08, 0.12, 0.18, 0.22, 0.30, 0.35, 0.42, 0.50, 0.60.
  • 3. The quantile. 20% should respond, so the threshold must sit at the 80th percentile, Qo(1−0.20)=Qo(0.80)Q_o(1 - 0.20) = Q_o(0.80)Qo​(1−0.20)=Qo​(0.80). With 10 values its position is 0.80 × 9 = 7.2 places from the bottom (counting from 0): between the 8th value (0.42) and the 9th (0.50), 20% of the way: 0.42 + 0.2 × (0.50 − 0.42) = 0.436.
  • 4. The gain. go=θ/Qo(0.80)=1/0.436g_o = \theta / Q_o(0.80) = 1 / 0.436go​=θ/Qo​(0.80)=1/0.436 = 2.294.
  • 5. Scaled drives xko=go∑gWkgrgox_{ko} = g_o \sum_g W_{kg} r_{go}xko​=go​∑g​Wkg​rgo​: 0.28, 0.69, 0.11, 0.96, 0.50, 0.41, 1.38, 0.80, 0.18, 1.15. Exactly two (from 0.60 and 0.50) are above 1, so 2 of 10 = 20% respond, as in TNT. The KC at 0.42 ends just below, at 0.96.

Dividing by the quantile only moves the threshold to the right place in each odor's distribution. The order of the KCs' drives (which KC responds) still comes from the connectome and the ORN responses. An odor with weak ORN responses has small drives, a small quantile, and therefore a large gain.

3.2Why the ratio is squared: (0.46/0.84)² ≈ 30%

A correlation r is not a share. Its square, r2r^2r2, is: the share of the data's variance that the model accounts for. The reasoning goes in three steps.

  • The data are part pattern, part noise. The split-half reliability of ΔS\Delta SΔS is 0.702: 70% of its variance over pairs is reproducible pattern, and 30% is recording noise that changes from one set of recordings to the next.
  • A perfect model can explain only the pattern. Its r2r^2r2 would be 0.702, so its r would be 0.702\sqrt{0.702}0.702​ = 0.838. That is the ceiling of 0.84.
  • The uniform model. r = 0.46, so r2r^2r2 = 0.207: it accounts for 21% of all the variance, which is 29% of the 70% that is pattern. That is r2/reliability=(r/ceiling)2r^2 / \text{reliability} = (r / \text{ceiling})^2r2/reliability=(r/ceiling)2.

A quick simulation confirms it: 120 mock pairs whose "data" are 70% pattern and 30% noise, and a mock model that shares 30% of its variance with the pattern. The model correlates with the noisy data at r = 0.45 on average and with the noise-free pattern at r = 0.54 (0.5520.55^20.552 = 0.30). The unsquared ratio 0.46/0.84 = 0.55 is that second correlation; squaring turns it into a share.

Figure 4 will get a y=xy = xy=x line in the rebuild (both axes are blocked ÷ intact ratios, so points on the line mean the model gets that odor's suppression right).

4Report 08: the inhibition rules

4.1The four rules as equations

All four rules start from the same pinned, blocked responses ykoblocked=[xko−1]+y^{\text{blocked}}_{ko} = [x_{ko} - 1]_+ykoblocked​=[xko​−1]+​ and all give the same mean fraction responding over odors (TNT3c's, 6.83%). They differ only in how the inhibition is shared out between odors. Your reading of the fixed rule is right.

The three extra rules are not new models of APL. They are controls that keep everything the same except how the inhibition depends on the odor: not at all (fixed), in proportion to the odor's own blocked response (same share), or exactly as in the data (TNT3c per odor). Comparing feedback with them shows that the odor-dependence created by feedback is what matters for the fit.

4.2How the Spearman values were computed, and -aPine's 1.71

For each of the 16 odors, two numbers, each the mean over the three mushroom bodies: the fraction responding with APL blocked (ϕoblocked\phi^{\text{blocked}}_oϕoblocked​, which equals the TNT fraction by pinning) and the gain γo=ϕoblocked/ϕointact\gamma_o = \phi^{\text{blocked}}_o / \phi^{\text{intact}}_oγo​=ϕoblocked​/ϕointact​. The Spearman correlation over the 16 odors between them is +0.96 for feedback and −0.62 for the fixed rule.

For -aPine, ϕblocked\phi^{\text{blocked}}ϕblocked = 6.07% and ϕintact\phi^{\text{intact}}ϕintact with feedback = 3.55%, so γ\gammaγ = 6.07 / 3.55 = 1.71, the smallest of the 16 (Report 08, Figure 1b, leftmost blue and orange points). In Figure 1a its blue dot is hidden under the orange diamond of the data, whose value is almost the same (1.70). Two things to fix in the rebuild: the dots will be drawn so none hides another, and γo\gamma_oγo​ will be called the "blocked ÷ intact ratio", because "gain" is also used for the input gain gog_ogo​ of Report 07. For -aPine that one is large, since its ORN responses are weak.

4.3Why odor strength was the mean of TNT and TNT3c, and the TNT-only result

I used the mean of the two conditions as a neutral measure of how strongly an odor drives the units, one that does not lean towards either condition. You are right that TNT alone is the better choice: TNT has no APL, so it measures the feed-forward drive directly, and it is also what the model's horizontal axis uses. TNT3c is already flattened by feedback, so mixing it in blurs the measure. The strength and the gain still come from separate halves of the recordings (4 TNT recordings for strength; the other 4 TNT and 6 of the TNT3c recordings for the gain), so they share no noise.

5Report 09: the noise correction

Equation 3 is Spearman's correction for attenuation. The logic, step by step:

  • 1. Every measurement is pattern + noise. The similarity of a pair measured from a set of recordings is its true value in that condition plus recording noise. A different set of recordings gives the same true value with different noise.
  • 2. Noise lowers correlations. If two measurements XXX and YYY each carry independent noise, their correlation is the correlation of their true values times a shrink factor: corr(X,Y)=corr(TX,TY)⋅relX relY\text{corr}(X, Y) = \text{corr}(T_X, T_Y) \cdot \sqrt{\text{rel}_X\,\text{rel}_Y}corr(X,Y)=corr(TX​,TY​)⋅relX​relY​​, where rel\text{rel}rel = (variance of the true values) ÷ (variance of the measurement) is the share of a measurement that is not noise.
  • 3. The within-condition correlation measures rel. Two halves of the same condition share the true values and differ only in noise, so their correlation equals rel: ρwithinTNT≈relTNT\rho^{\text{TNT}}_{\text{within}} \approx \text{rel}_{\text{TNT}}ρwithinTNT​≈relTNT​, and the same for TNT3c.
  • 4. Undo the shrink. ρbetween\rho_{\text{between}}ρbetween​ (a TNT half against a TNT3c half) is the true TNT-vs-TNT3c correlation shrunk by relTNT relTNT3c\sqrt{\text{rel}_{\text{TNT}}\,\text{rel}_{\text{TNT3c}}}relTNT​relTNT3c​​. Dividing by that factor gives Equation 3.
  • 5. Why halves on both sides. The between value is computed from half-size samples, exactly like the within values, so both carry the same amount of noise and no Spearman–Brown step is needed.

In the second row the between value drops to about 0.83, as in the data, and the correction recovers the true value.

6Report 11: the local APL model

6.1θ in Equation 1

Yes, θ = 1. Because each odor's input is pinned (Report 07), the threshold can be any positive number: the gains gog_ogo​ scale the inputs to it. Setting θ = 1 just fixes the units, so xkox_{ko}xko​ is measured in "threshold units" (1 = exactly at threshold).

6.2Equation 3, every variable, with a mock tree

What it computes. For the local model we need Φvj\Phi_{vj}Φvj​: the total signal that KC jjj's inputs to APL produce at a point vvv of APL, each input decayed by its distance along APL, Φvj=∑t∈in(j)e−d(v,t)/λ\Phi_{vj} = \sum_{t \in \text{in}(j)} e^{-d(v,t)/\lambda}Φvj​=∑t∈in(j)​e−d(v,t)/λ. Summing it over KC kkk's output sites gives MkjM_{kj}Mkj​. Equation 3 computes Φ\PhiΦ for every node without ever listing distances, using one fact: the decay along a path is the product of the decays of its edges, e−(ℓ1+ℓ2)/λ=e−ℓ1/λ e−ℓ2/λe^{-(\ell_1 + \ell_2)/\lambda} = e^{-\ell_1/\lambda}\,e^{-\ell_2/\lambda}e−(ℓ1​+ℓ2​)/λ=e−ℓ1​/λe−ℓ2​/λ.

6.3The C matrix

Yes, it is the same per-KC weighting as version C of Reports 05 and 07, written as a matrix: Mkj=uk vj/NM_{kj} = u_k\,v_j / NMkj​=uk​vj​/N, with uku_kuk​ = KC kkk's APL→KC synapses and vjv_jvj​ = KC jjj's KC→APL synapses in the calyx, each divided by its mean. Putting it into Equation 1 gives a∑jMkj yjo=a uk⋅1N∑jvj yjo=a uk Aoa\sum_j M_{kj}\,y_{jo} = a\,u_k \cdot \frac{1}{N}\sum_j v_j\,y_{jo} = a\,u_k\,A_oa∑j​Mkj​yjo​=auk​⋅N1​∑j​vj​yjo​=auk​Ao​, which is exactly version C: one APL activity AoA_oAo​ (the vvv-weighted mean KC response), applied to KC kkk in proportion to uku_kuk​. M is "C" only to compare it with the local matrices, which have the same form but let the coupling depend on where on APL the synapses are.
